now.title: pets.com
now.text: The .com registry shows the domain was first registered in November 1994, four years before the company was incorporated. PetSmart.com bought the domain names in December 2000, and a Wayback capture of Dec 28, 2025 shows pets.com redirecting to petsmart.com. The sale list also included defensive names such as ihatepets.com and petscomsucks.com.

now.title: The Pets.com trademarks
now.text: All five 1999 applications checked at the USPTO (PETS.COM, BECAUSE PETS CAN'T DRIVE, MORE PRODUCTS THAN A SUPERSTORE. DELIVERY TO YOUR DOOR, KEEP IT COMIN' and EVERYTHING THEY NEED) are abandoned, from July 2000 to January 2002. The owner of record on PETS.COM is still Pets.com, Inc.
now.note: Do not write "no one owns the trademark": registrations filed later by others were not searchable (gap pc-145).

now.title: The sock puppet
now.text: Pets.com signed an exclusive agent in March 2000 and six licensees by September. In 2001 the estate collected $125,000 from Hakan Enterprises for all rights to the puppet. At the end of 2001 licensee Fun4All still owed $153,811 in royalties; the estate sued in June 2002. 1-800-Bar None launched the puppet as its spokesperson in May 2002.

now.title: IPET Holdings, the estate
now.text: Renamed IPET Holdings and dissolved Jan 18, 2001, with Diablo Management Group running the liquidation under Richard G. Couch. Net assets in liquidation fell from $58.7M at the start of liquidation to $9.6M at Dec 31, 2000 and $4.2M a year later. Stockholders received $0.09, $0.075 and $0.00747 a share, and the company terminated its registration with a Form 15 dated Jun 3, 2005.

now.title: Julie Wainwright
now.text: The Pets.com CEO later founded The RealReal. She resigned as its CEO, chairperson and director on Jun 6, 2022, effective Jun 7, after 11 years, and stayed on as an adviser through the end of 2022.

now.title: Amazon's stake

now.title: The idea, at Chewy
now.text: Chewy reported fiscal 2025 net sales of $12.60 billion, a 29.8% gross margin and 21.3 million active customers. Autoship customers made up 83.3% of net sales, against 79.2% a year earlier.

glossary.def: Sales minus the cost of goods sold, usually shown as a share of sales. What counts as a cost of goods sold varies by company.
The costs a company books directly against the products it sells. Whether shipping, warehouse labor and delivery belong here is a choice each company makes and discloses.
Storing, picking, packing and shipping orders. For an online retailer it is usually its own cost line or part of another one.
Statements prepared for a company that is winding down. Assets are shown at what they are expected to fetch and there is no profit and loss, only changes in net assets.
What is expected to be left for owners after the estate sells assets and pays its debts.
The filing that legally ends a Delaware corporation, which can then only wind up its affairs.
A short SEC filing in which a large shareholder reports how much of a company it owns.
The registration statement a company files with the SEC before selling shares to the public.
The filing that ends a company's duty to file periodic reports with the SEC.
Financial statements shown as if a deal had already happened, with adjustments to make two companies' books comparable.
Chewy's name for scheduled repeat deliveries. Pets.com, PETsMART.com and Petopia each described an equivalent program in their filings.

insights.summary: Pets.com's gross margin never included fulfillment. Its filings book fulfillment and distribution in marketing and sales, so the improvement from −20% (Q2 2000) to −3% (Q3 2000) measured products plus shipping only, and Q3 also included a one-time shipping charge adjustment of about $631,000 (6.7% of Q3 net sales, derived; the filing does not say which way it moved the margin). A rival's books show how much that left out: Pets.com's own pro forma moved $2,959K of Petstore.com's 1999 fulfillment cost (57% of its cost of sales, 141% of its net sales) and $3,974K in H1 2000 (39% of cost of sales, 91% of net sales) out of cost of sales, which turned Petstore.com's 1999 gross margin from −146% to about −5%. Webvan and Kozmo draw the line differently again: Webvan kept $64.4M of 2000 warehouse and delivery costs in G&A (36% of its $178.5M sales; its 26.5% gross margin becomes about −10% if they are added to cost of goods sold, derived), and Kozmo's 43% 1999 gross profit sat above $3.3M of delivery payroll booked as an operating expense. So the three headline gross margins are not comparable, and Pets.com's true cost of getting a box to the door cannot be read from any of its filings (the filings give no fulfillment dollar amount; gap pc-143). No filing records a change in classification between 1999 and 2000 (gap pc-164), so the −132% to −3% move is not an accounting artifact, but it is not the full cost of delivery either.

insights.summary: In 1999 three of the four pet e-tailers (Petstore.com's offering was not checked) ran scheduled repeat delivery, so a subscription program did not separate them from each other: Pets.com "Keep It Comin'", PETsMART.com "You Sit, We Fetch" and Petopia "Bottomless Bowl", which Petopia said produced a significant portion of its revenue. What separated them in their S-1s was how much they sold per dollar of marketing and how the product reached the door: PETsMART.com sold $10.4M against Pets.com's $5.8M (1.8×) with $33.5M against $42.5M of sales and marketing, and a gross margin of −60% against −132%, with substantially all orders fulfilled by its partner PETsMART, Inc. Even so PETsMART.com lost $47.5M in the year. The page's Chewy comparison ("built on subscriptions") should say that the subscription idea already appears in the three filings checked.

insights.summary: What the estate paid out against what it held. Net assets in liquidation were $58.7M when liquidation began on Nov 5, 2000. By Dec 31, 2000 they were $9.6M after $45.8M of net write-offs and disposals (fixed assets $18.9M, 5,243,752 shares recovered in settling an advertising agreement $8.1M, prepaid advertising $7.0M, inventory $4.8M, equity stakes $5.7M, other prepaids $2.5M) and about $3.3M of net cash use. Stockholders then received $0.172 a share in three payments, about $6.0M on 34.7M shares (derived), or 7.3% of the $82.5M raised in the IPO. During liquidation the estate also paid $4.2M of retention, severance and other compensation (Nov–Dec 2000), $1.0M on leases it was no longer using (2001) and about $550K to end the Union City sublease (2002). The 10-K's use-of-proceeds section separately reports $1.4M of retention bonuses and $1.4M of severance to ten officers.
